passage: Every time Vijay Chacha came over from the next village, the talk at the handpump went the same way. 'Preeti, twenty-one already. By twenty-three you should be married. And do B.Ed, it's safe, teachers get respect.' Preeti smiled and kept filling the matka. She loved him. He had carried her on his shoulders at the Dussehra mela; he had paid for her first cycle. That was what made it hard. She had already filled in the form for the two-year agriculture diploma at the college in Hisar and hadn't told anyone. That evening, while he drank his tea, she sat beside him on the charpai. 'Chachaji, I know you say it because you worry for me. I'm listening. And I want to show you something I've chosen.' She held out the form. He read it slowly, frowning, and didn't say no.

qa.q: Which course had Preeti filled in the form for?
qa.a: The two-year agriculture diploma at the college in Hisar.

qa.q: Why does Preeti find Vijay Chacha's advice hard to push back on?
qa.a: Preeti loves him and remembers his care, the mela and the cycle, so the pressure comes wrapped in affection, and saying no feels like hurting him.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti make that kept both respect and her own decision?
qa.a: She sat beside him, named his worry as love, said she was listening, and then showed her own form, so he felt respected without her giving up the diploma.

qa.q: How might Vijay Chacha feel reading the form?
qa.a: He may feel surprised and a little uneasy that his plan isn't hers, but also touched that she brought it to him first, which may be why he frowns and doesn't say no.

grounding: Shows a young woman who hears repeated shoulds about marriage age and a course from a loving uncle, and answers with respect while holding to her own choice.

passage: Sunday call from Chengdu, 9 p.m. in Vancouver. Xin put her mother on speaker while she chopped bok choy. 'You should switch to accounting, it's stable. And you should meet the Li family's son when you're home. At twenty-five I was already married.' 'Mm-hm,' Xin said. 'Mm-hm.' Nadia, her roommate, watched Xin's knife slow down. After the call, Xin sat on the kitchen floor. 'She sends me dried mushrooms every month. She saved for years so I could come here. How do I say no to someone like that?' Nadia sat beside her. 'Maybe you don't say no to her. You say no to the plan.' Xin thought about it for a long time. The next Sunday she said, 'Ma, I love that you think about my future. I'm staying in urban planning. Now tell me about your garden.'

qa.q: What does Xin's mother send every month?
qa.a: She sends Xin dried mushrooms every month.

qa.q: What does Xin's slowing knife suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the call is weighing on Xin: the shoulds about accounting and marriage bring pressure, even as Xin feels grateful for everything her mother gave up.

qa.q: What turning point helped Xin answer differently the next Sunday?
qa.a: Nadia's idea of saying no to the plan rather than to the person let Xin thank her mother for caring while clearly staying in urban planning.

qa.q: How might Xin's mother experience the new reply?
qa.a: She may be disappointed about accounting, but hearing love named first and being asked about her garden could help her feel respected rather than pushed away.

grounding: Shows a young woman abroad who hears constant shoulds about her course and marriage from a loving mother, and learns to reply with warmth and her own choice.

passage: Visiting day at the engineering hostel meant plastic chairs in the warden's hall, and Urmila Bua had brought a steel tiffin of besan laddoos. 'Sumit, you should finish B.Tech, then MBA. And by twenty-six you should be settled. I've already seen a girl's photo, very nice family.' Sumit took a laddoo. He wanted to tell her about the music society, how he'd been composing for the college band and thinking of a sound engineering course after graduation. But she had come three hours by bus. She had wrapped each laddoo in paper. 'Bua, these are exactly like last year's,' he said, and meant it. Then, carefully: 'I'll finish B.Tech, I promise. After that I want to try sound engineering. Can I play you something next time?' She blinked. 'Sound what?' But she didn't close the tiffin until he'd explained.

qa.q: How far had Urmila Bua travelled for visiting day?
qa.a: Urmila Bua had come three hours by bus.

qa.q: Why does Sumit hesitate before mentioning the music society?
qa.a: Sumit feels Bua's love in the long bus ride and the wrapped laddoos, so voicing a different plan feels like it might hurt her; affection and pressure arrive together.

qa.q: Which part of Sumit's reply kept respect and his own choice together?
qa.a: He agreed to finish B.Tech, which honours her wish, while naming sound engineering clearly and inviting her to hear his music, so it became a conversation instead of a fight.

qa.q: How might Urmila Bua see Sumit's plan at first?
qa.a: She may find 'sound engineering' strange and worry it is less secure, but staying to listen suggests she wants to understand her nephew, not only instruct him.

grounding: Shows a hostel student receiving loving shoulds about courses and marriage from his aunt, and answering with respect while stating his own plan.

passage:
Dear Salma Phuppo,

Thank you for the shawl. I'm wearing it right now in the hostel, and it still smells of your almirah.

I want to answer what you said on the phone on Sunday, because I just said "ji, ji" and then cried a bit after.

You said I should be married by twenty-three, like you were. You said I should switch from journalism to nursing because it's "safe for a girl". I know you say these things because you love me. You were the one who taught me to read the Urdu newspaper, word by word, on your verandah. That's partly why I'm studying journalism at all.

So I feel two things at once: grateful and squeezed.

I'm not switching. I'd like to finish this degree and work for a while before I think about marriage. I hope you can still be proud of me. I'll call you on Eid and tell you about my first article.

With love and respect,
Kiran

qa.q: What did Salma Phuppo say Kiran should switch to?
qa.a: She said Kiran should switch from journalism to nursing.

qa.q: What does Kiran mean by feeling "grateful and squeezed"?
qa.a: Kiran loves Phuppo and knows the advice comes from care, but the constant shoulds also feel like pressure. Both feelings are real at the same time.

qa.q: What choice does Kiran make in the letter, and why is it a respectful one?
qa.a: Kiran decides to stay with journalism and wait on marriage, but says it warmly, thanks Phuppo, and links her own choice to what Phuppo taught her. She keeps the relationship while keeping her decision.

qa.q: How might Salma Phuppo feel reading that her Urdu lessons led Kiran to journalism?
qa.a: Phuppo might feel touched and proud, and also a little torn, since the path she worries about grew from her own teaching. It could soften the pressure she puts on Kiran.

grounding: A young woman hears repeated shoulds from her aunt about marriage age and course choice, feels love and pressure together, and answers with respect and her own choice.

passage:
Hafsa, you asked why I went quiet when my phone buzzed. It was Aai. It's always Aai at 8 p.m.

Every call has the same three shoulds. "Nitin, you should do MBA, not this design course. You should be settled by twenty-six. You should come home more." And the funny part is, I don't even disagree with the last one.

I love her so much it's annoying. She worked double shifts at the textile mill so I could come to Pune. So when she says "should", it doesn't feel like an order. It feels like a debt.

For a year I just said "ho, Aai" and changed nothing. Then I felt guilty and angry at the same time.

Last week I tried something new. I said, "Aai, I hear you. I'm going to finish design. I'll come home every second Sunday." She was quiet. Then she said, "Every second Sunday. Promise."

She didn't agree about design. But she heard me.

qa.q: How often did Nitin promise to come home?
qa.a: Every second Sunday.

qa.q: Why does Aai's "should" feel like a debt to Nitin rather than an order?
qa.a: Nitin knows Aai worked double shifts at the mill so Nitin could study in Pune, so disagreeing feels like being ungrateful. Love and pressure are tangled together.

qa.q: What was the turning point in how Nitin handled Aai's shoulds?
qa.a: Instead of saying "ho, Aai" and changing nothing, Nitin told Aai "I hear you", stated a clear choice about design, and offered something real, coming home every second Sunday. It kept respect and choice together.

qa.q: How might Aai feel after Nitin's new answer?
qa.a: Aai may still be worried about the design course, but reassured that Nitin will come home and is being honest with her. Her "Promise" suggests she took what she could hold on to.

grounding: A young adult hears constant shoulds from Aai about course and settling down, feels love and pressure together, and finds a way to keep both respect and personal choice.
